content: Malachite green, also known as aniline green, basic green 4, diamond green B, or victoria green B, is a toxic chemical primarily used as a dye. Its IUPAC name is 4-N,N-dimethyl-aniline. When diluted, it can serve as a topical antiseptic and is used to treat parasitic, fungal, and bacterial infections in fish and fish eggs. Additionally, it is employed as a bacteriological stain. However, in 1992, Canadian authorities determined that consuming fish contaminated with malachite green posed significant health risks to humans. The chemical was classified as a Class II Health Hazard due to its toxicity to human cells and its potential to induce liver tumor formation. Despite these risks, malachite green continues to be used in some countries with less stringent regulations for non-aquaculture purposes because of its low cost and ease of production. In 2005, traces of malachite green were detected in eels and fish imported from China and Taiwan into Hong Kong. Similarly, in 2006, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) found malachite green in seafood imported from China, where its use in aquaculture is also banned. By June 2007, the FDA blocked the importation of several seafood varieties due to continued contamination with malachite green. The substance has been banned in the United States for food-related applications since 1983. Malachite green exists in a chromatic form, which is a green dye. However, when absorbed into the body, it is metabolized into other forms. The first is the carbinol form, which crosses cell membranes more rapidly. Once inside the cell, it is further metabolized into leuco-malachite green, a form known to be toxic and retained in the body for longer periods than the chromatic form. This prolonged retention raises concerns about its safety. Malachite green is widely used to dye materials such as silk, leather, and paper. Despite its name, it does not contain the mineral malachite; the name is derived from the similarity in color. It is particularly effective against the fungus Saprolegnia, which infects fish eggs in commercial aquaculture, and is also a popular treatment for Ichthyophthirius infections in freshwater aquariums. However, its principal metabolite, leuco-malachite green (LMG), is retained in fish muscle tissues for extended periods, making it the main chemical found in fish treated with malachite green. This has led to its ban in many countries due to its suspected carcinogenic properties. Laboratory tests have shown that rats fed malachite green at concentrations of 100 parts per billion (ppb) for over two years developed tumors. Furthermore, malachite green is highly toxic to certain freshwater fish species, such as tetras, catfish, and shark catfish. It is strongly recommended to use half-dosages when treating tanks containing these sensitive species. Malachite green is also used as a biological stain for microscopic analysis of cells and tissues. In the Gimenez staining method, it serves as a blue-green counterstain, while basic fuchsin stains bacteria red or magenta. Additionally, malachite green can directly stain endospores within cells, often with a safranin counterstain. However, this application is relatively rare. Leuco-malachite green is also employed in forensic science as a detection method for latent blood. Hemoglobin catalyzes the reaction between LMG and hydrogen peroxide, converting the colorless LMG into the chromatic form of malachite green, with the appearance of a green color indicating the presence of blood. When used in aquatic animals, malachite green is metabolized into leuco-malachite green. The toxicity of malachite green in fish is influenced by factors such as water hardness, pH, temperature, and dissolved oxygen levels. Studies have shown that its toxicity increases with rising temperatures or decreasing pH. Research on fish eggs has demonstrated that doubling the concentration of malachite green can increase the mortality rate of rainbow trout eggs by up to 20 times, indicating its extreme toxicity to certain fish species and especially to fish eggs. Other reported effects include carcinogenesis, mutagenesis, and reduced fertility in rainbow trout. While malachite green is highly effective against fungal and parasitic infections in fish, it also causes significant adverse effects. Malachite green and its major metabolite, leuco-malachite green, have been reported to exhibit mutagenic and carcinogenic effects. Recent studies, such as those by Culp SJ, have shown that rats fed malachite green experience a dose-related increase in liver DNA adducts and lung adenomas. Leuco-malachite green has been found to increase the number and severity of cellular changes. Since leuco-malachite green is the primary metabolite of malachite green and is retained in fish muscle for longer periods, most human intake of malachite green occurs in its leuco form. Experiments have shown that rats fed up to 543 ppm of leuco-malachite green—an extreme amount compared to the average 5 ppb found in fish—developed lung adenomas after two years, though no liver tumors were observed. This suggests that malachite green may cause carcinogenic symptoms, but a direct link to liver tumors has not been conclusively established. In 2005, investigations by the Hong Kong Government Labs revealed traces of malachite green in freshwater fish, crabs, and other aquaculture products from China. Later, saltwater fish from China and Taiwan were also found to contain this toxin. However, Taiwanese officials disputed these findings, asserting that malachite green had long been banned in Taiwan. Hong Kong’s Food & Environmental Hygiene Department confirmed that 11 out of 14 eel-based products tested from local supermarkets contained high levels of malachite green. Despite this, the concentrations found in seafood were relatively low, with the highest levels detected being 4,500 μg/kg in eels and 900 μg/kg in freshwater fish.
